Many groups in Nigeria call themselves a cooperative: a thrift group, a market women's association, a farmers' union, a set of tailors sharing one shop. Some of them truly are cooperatives. Others are a business owned by one strong person with friends helping. The difference matters, because the cooperative model gives members rights that the other models do not. This lesson gives you the exact standard used around the world, so you can test your own group against it.

A cooperative is people, not capital: the members own it, control it and use it.
The definition

The International Cooperative Alliance (ICA) is the global body for cooperatives. Its Statement on the Cooperative Identity, revised in 1995, defines a cooperative as: **"an autonomous association of persons united voluntarily to meet their common economic, social and cultural needs and aspirations through a jointly-owned and democratically-controlled enterprise."** Read it slowly, because every phrase is a test.
**Autonomous:** the group runs itself. A politician, a donor or a buyer may support it, but does not control it.
**Association of persons:** it is built around people, not around money. The member with the biggest share does not own more of the decisions.
**United voluntarily:** nobody is forced to join or forced to stay.
**Common economic, social and cultural needs:** members join to meet real shared needs, such as cheaper inputs, a bigger market, training or mutual support.
**Jointly-owned and democratically-controlled enterprise:** it is a real business, owned together and governed by the members.
The values

The ICA statement says cooperatives are based on six values: **self-help, self-responsibility, democracy, equality, equity and solidarity.** Members also hold four ethical values: **honesty, openness, social responsibility and caring for others.** Notice the difference between equality and equity. Equality means every member has the same rights, for example one vote each. Equity means fairness in how members are treated and rewarded, for example sharing surplus according to how much each member used or worked for the cooperative.

The principles are the guidelines by which cooperatives put their values into practice. Below is each one in plain words, with what it looks like in a Nigerian group enterprise.

Surplus, not profit

Cooperatives often say surplus instead of profit. The idea is that money left after costs came from the members' own business with the cooperative, so it is returned or reinvested by member decision, not paid out to outside investors.

A group can work together for years without registering anything. That is fine while the money is small. Once the group signs contracts, opens a bank account, borrows, or applies for a grant, the question of legal form becomes urgent: who signs, who owns the equipment, and who pays if something goes wrong? This lesson compares the main options open to a Nigerian women's group enterprise and gives you a readiness check to run before you choose.

Check current requirements yourself

Registration requirements, minimum membership numbers and fees differ between states and change over time. Before you register a cooperative society, visit your state's cooperative office in person and ask for the current list of documents and fees in writing. Do not pay an agent who cannot show you an official receipt.
Who carries the risk

In an informal group, if the treasurer signs for a 2 million naira fabric order on credit and the buyer then cancels, the supplier can chase the treasurer personally. Many groups only discover this when it happens. A registered cooperative or a company can enter the contract in its own name, so the obligation sits with the entity, though officers can still be held responsible for fraud or for acting outside their authority. This is the main reason to register once the stakes rise.

A cooperative society also suits a group that wants the cooperative principles written into law: one member, one vote, and surplus returned to members according to their use of the business. A company suits a group where a few people invest most of the capital and expect control in proportion. Many women's groups that start as friends sharing work choose the cooperative route for this reason. Some funders and government programmes also prefer to work with registered groups, but read each programme's own rules rather than assuming.

Registration does not create trust; it only gives trust a legal shape. Before registering, or before accepting an order bigger than the group has handled, score the group on eight points. Bylaws are the rule book of a cooperative. A registered cooperative society must have them, and an informal group should write something very similar as its group agreement. Good bylaws are dull to write and priceless in a crisis. When a member is accused of taking money, when two women both want to be chairperson, or when a big order arrives and someone wants to change the profit sharing, the group opens the bylaws instead of shouting.
A person holding a signed document
Bylaws turn verbal promises into rules every member signed up to.
What the bylaws must cover
**Name, address and objects:** what the cooperative exists to do, for example "to produce and market hand-dyed textiles for members".
**Membership:** who may join, how to apply, entry fee and minimum share, rights and duties, and how membership ends (resignation, death, expulsion).
**General meetings:** the annual general meeting (AGM), how special meetings are called, notice period, quorum and voting.
**Management committee and officers:** positions, how they are elected, term length, maximum number of terms, and how to remove them.
**Money:** share capital, bank account and signatories, spending limits, records, audit, and how surplus is allocated.
**Disputes and discipline:** the steps for complaints, fines and expulsion, and the right to be heard.
**Amendment and dissolution:** how bylaws are changed, and what happens to assets if the cooperative closes.
Authority flows upward from members

In a cooperative the highest authority is the general meeting of all members. The general meeting elects a management committee. The committee appoints or supervises officers and any staff who run daily work. Many cooperatives also elect a small supervisory or audit committee that checks the books on members' behalf. Write this chain into the bylaws so that nobody, not even the founder, sits above the general meeting.
Who answers to whom
General meeting of all members
Elected management committee
Supervisory or audit committee
Officers and staff
The members at the top hold final power; every level below reports back to them.
Quorum and voting

A **quorum** is the minimum number of members who must be present for a meeting's decisions to count. Without one, three members could meet on a quiet afternoon and decide to sell the group's machine. An **ordinary resolution** passes by a simple majority of members present and voting. A **special resolution**, needed for serious matters, requires a larger majority, often two-thirds. Your bylaws should list which decisions are special. Common ones are changing the bylaws, borrowing above a set amount, selling major equipment, expelling a member, and dissolving the cooperative.
Worked example: setting quorum and a two-thirds rule

For example, a 24-member palm oil processing cooperative near Owerri is drafting its bylaws. The secretary, Ngozi, proposes a quorum of half the members plus one, and a two-thirds majority of members present for special resolutions.
Quorum: half of 24 is 12, plus one is 13. At least 13 members must be present.
At the meeting, 18 members are present, so quorum is met.
The committee proposes buying a second press on credit, which the bylaws list as a special resolution.
Two-thirds of 18 present is 18 x 2 / 3 = 12. The motion needs at least 12 yes votes.
The vote is 13 yes, 4 no and 1 abstention. 13 is at least 12, so the motion passes.
Ngozi records in the minutes: members present, quorum met, motion text, and the vote count.
The decision is valid and recorded. If only 12 members had come, the meeting would have had no quorum and the press purchase would have had to wait for a properly called meeting.
Money rules that prevent most quarrels
All money goes into the cooperative's bank account. No officer keeps group money in a personal account.
Every payment needs two signatories or two approvals on the banking app, and the two must not be related or from the same household.
Spending limits: officers may spend up to a fixed amount per month for routine costs; above it, the committee decides; above a higher amount, the general meeting decides.
Every naira in or out is written in the cashbook with a receipt or bank reference, and any member may inspect the books on request.
Surplus is allocated each year by the general meeting according to the bylaw rule, for example a fixed percentage to reserves first.
Protect members' money from fraud

Never share the group account's banking app PIN or one-time passwords in the WhatsApp group, even with officers. Each signatory keeps her own login. Scammers often pose as bank staff or as a member who has "changed her number". Confirm any unusual payment request by a voice call to a number already saved, and report suspected fraud to your bank at once.
Limit terms of office

A rule such as "officers serve two years and may be re-elected once" gives new members a path into leadership and stops one person becoming the cooperative. Write it in before anyone has been in office long enough to resist it.

Separation of duties

**Separation of duties** means that the steps of any money process are split between at least two people, so that an error or a theft by one person is likely to be noticed by another. The classic split is: one person approves a payment, another makes it, and a third records it or checks the records. In a small group of 8 to 15 women you cannot always have three people, but you can always have two. The treasurer pays; the financial secretary records; the supervisory committee checks monthly that the two agree.
Controls protect the honest

Separation of duties is not an accusation. It protects an honest treasurer from being suspected, because the records show what happened. Explain it to members this way and it is accepted much more easily.
A standard operating procedure for an order

A **standard operating procedure (SOP)** is a short written list of the steps for a task that happens again and again, with who does each step. Write one for your most common money flow: from the moment a customer asks for a price to the moment the group is paid in full. Keep it to one page so it can be pinned up or shared as a picture on the group's WhatsApp.
Worked example: an order SOP for a catering group

For example, Hauwa's 9-member catering cooperative in Kaduna receives a request to supply 200 plates of jollof rice with chicken for a wedding, at 3,500 naira per plate (an illustrative price; check current local prices).
Sales lead (Aisha) confirms the menu, quantity, date and price on WhatsApp and sends a written quote: 200 x 3,500 = 700,000 naira, 60 percent deposit to confirm.
Customer pays the deposit of 700,000 x 0.60 = 420,000 naira by transfer into the cooperative's bank account only. Aisha never accepts it into her own account.
Treasurer (Rakiya) confirms the credit on the bank app and tells the group the order is confirmed.
Financial secretary (Zainab) records the deposit in the cashbook and the order register, with the bank reference.
Production lead (Hauwa) writes the ingredient list and work rota. Purchases above the officers' limit are approved by a second committee member before Rakiya pays.
Production lead checks food safety on the day: clean hands, covered hair, food held hot, no member cooking while sick.
Balance of 280,000 naira is collected by transfer before the food is served, recorded by Zainab, and the customer gets a receipt.

Five different members touched the order, each with a clear duty. The money never passed through a personal account, every naira has a bank reference, and any member can trace the order from quote to full payment.

Food orders

For any group that cooks or processes food, add hygiene steps to the SOP: hand washing with soap, clean water, separating raw and cooked foods, cooking thoroughly and keeping food at safe temperatures. These follow the WHO Five Keys to Safer Food. A member with diarrhoea or vomiting should not handle food that day.

Some groups rotate roles to share skills and avoid power building up in one person. That is healthy, provided each period has a named holder and a proper handover. When the treasurer changes, the outgoing and incoming treasurers, with one committee member, count any cash, print or screenshot the bank balance, agree the cashbook balance, and all three sign a short handover note. Without this, problems from the old term become arguments in the new one.

Describe what a supervisory committee checks each month

A buyer who orders from a group expects the same quality whoever made the item. In a single-owner business, the standard lives in the owner's head. In a group it must be written down and checked, or one member's weak work damages everyone's name. The same is true of money: members trust the books only if someone other than the person keeping them checks them regularly. This lesson covers both kinds of check.
A clipboard for inspection notes
A written specification and a short inspection record make quality the same for every member's work.
The product specification sheet

A **specification sheet** describes exactly what a finished product must be. It should be specific enough that two members checking the same item would reach the same verdict. For a sewn school uniform, it might list: fabric type and colour code, measurements for each size with an allowed difference of about 1 cm, stitch type and stitches per inch, buttons sewn with a shank, no loose threads, pressed and folded, size label attached. For a food or cosmetic product, it includes the recipe, batch size, packing and labelling. Products sold packaged to the public in Nigeria may also need NAFDAC registration; check with NAFDAC before selling in shops.
Inspection and a fair process
The production lead, or a rotating inspector, checks a sample from each member's batch against the specification before delivery. For small orders, check every piece.
Record the result in an inspection log: date, member, number checked, number passed, fault found.
Return faulty pieces to the member privately with the specific fault named, for example "hem uneven by 2 cm", and a date to correct it.
If the same member fails twice in a row, the production lead pairs her with a stronger member for the next batch.
Repeated failure after support goes to the committee under the discipline clause in the bylaws, never to public criticism on WhatsApp.

The monthly bank reconciliation

A **bank reconciliation** compares the group's own cashbook balance with the balance on the bank statement for the same date, and explains every difference. The two rarely match exactly, for honest reasons: bank charges and SMS alerts the bookkeeper has not yet recorded, a member's transfer that reached the bank but was not written in the cashbook, or a deposit made on the last day that the bank shows the next day. The job is to adjust both sides until they agree. If a difference remains that nobody can explain, it must be investigated before the meeting, not ignored.
Worked example: reconciling September
For example, Grace is on the supervisory committee of a 15-member uniform sewing cooperative in Jos. On 30 September the cashbook shows 412,500 naira, but the bank statement shows 389,000 naira.
Bank charges and SMS fees on the statement, not in the cashbook: 1,500 naira. Cashbook adjusted: 412,500 - 1,500 = 411,000.
A member's share payment of 20,000 naira arrived in the bank but was not recorded. Cashbook adjusted: 411,000 + 20,000 = 431,000.
A deposit of 45,000 naira paid in on 30 September shows on the bank statement only on 1 October. Bank side adjusted: 389,000 + 45,000 = 434,000.
Difference remaining: 434,000 - 431,000 = 3,000 naira. Grace checks the cashbook line by line.
She finds a 3,000 naira payment for thread written twice. Removing the duplicate adds 3,000 back: 431,000 + 3,000 = 434,000.
Both sides now show 434,000 naira. Grace and the financial secretary both sign the reconciliation sheet.
The September books are reconciled at 434,000 naira, with every difference explained in writing. The bookkeeper corrects the duplicate entry and records the bank charges and the member's payment.
When a difference cannot be explained

If money is missing after checking every line, do not accuse anyone in the group chat. The supervisory committee writes down the facts, asks the officers concerned for an explanation in a private meeting, and reports to the next general meeting. If fraud is suspected, involve the bank and take advice from your state cooperative office.

Group money needs extra clarity because several households depend on it. The most common money quarrels in group enterprises are not about theft. They are about a price that did not cover costs, an order the group could not finish on time, or a surplus shared in a way some members felt was unfair. This lesson works through all three with one realistic order, using the cooperative rule for sharing surplus from Principle 3.
An abacus for counting
Cost first, check capacity second, share surplus last, and write every figure down.
Step 1: Cost the whole order

List every cost the group will pay to deliver the order: materials, members' labour paid per piece or per day, transport, electricity or fuel for machines, packaging, and bank or payment fees. Members' labour is a real cost. If the price only covers materials, members are working for nothing and the surplus is an illusion. The difference between the order value and the total cost is the **surplus**.
Step 2: Check capacity honestly

Group capacity is not simply the sum of what each member can do alone. Coordination, waiting for shared machines, inspection and corrections all take time. Add a buffer of about 20 percent to the pure production time, and compare the result with the delivery date before saying yes.
Step 3: Allocate the surplus by the bylaws

The ICA's third principle says members allocate surpluses to developing the cooperative (possibly through reserves, at least part of which is indivisible), to benefiting members in proportion to their transactions with the cooperative, and to other activities the members approve. The payment to members in proportion to their transactions is often called a **patronage refund**. In a producers' group, a member's transactions can be the number of pieces she produced or the produce she supplied. Your bylaws fix the percentages. The ones below are illustrative choices for this example, not legal requirements; check whether your state's cooperative rules set a minimum reserve.
Worked example: 300 school uniform sets

For example, the 6 sewing members of Bisola's cooperative in Ibadan are offered an order of 300 uniform sets at 6,500 naira per set, delivery in 15 working days. All prices are illustrative; use your own current local prices.
Order value: 300 x 6,500 = 1,950,000 naira.
Materials per set: fabric 2,400 + thread, buttons and zip 350 + packaging 100 = 2,850 naira. For 300 sets: 855,000 naira.
Sewing labour paid to members: 1,500 per set x 300 = 450,000 naira. Cutting: 200 per set x 300 = 60,000 naira.
Transport and delivery 40,000, fuel and machine maintenance 60,000, bank and transfer fees 5,000 naira.
Capacity: 6 members x 5 sets a day = 30 sets a day. 300 / 30 = 10 days, plus a 20 percent buffer = 12 days. That fits within 15 days, so the group accepts.
Allocation by the bylaws: reserve 25 percent = 120,000; education and training fund 5 percent = 24,000; patronage refund 70 percent = 336,000 naira. Check: 120,000 + 24,000 + 336,000 = 480,000.
Patronage per set: 336,000 / 300 = 1,120 naira for each set a member sewed.

The order makes a surplus of 480,000 naira. 120,000 builds the reserve, 24,000 pays for training, and 336,000 is returned to the six sewing members at 1,120 naira per set they produced, on top of the labour pay they already received.

A well-run group is attractive to bigger buyers, distributors and programmes, because it offers more capacity than a single producer. That attention is good news, but large offers often come with terms that can sink a small cooperative: long payment delays, exclusivity, penalties, or a partner who wants a say in how the group is run. Principle 4 says any agreement with an outside organisation must keep democratic control by the members and the cooperative's autonomy. This lesson shows how to test an offer before members vote on it.
Two people shaking hands on a deal
A good deal is one the group can deliver, afford to wait for, and still control.
Four questions for every big offer
**Cash:** How much must the group spend before the first payment arrives? Do we have it, without borrowing at high cost?
**Capacity:** Can we produce this quantity, to the standard, with a 20 percent time buffer?
**Control:** Does any clause give the partner power over our members, officers, prices to others, or bylaws?
**Exit:** Can either side end the agreement with reasonable notice, and what happens to goods already made?
Working capital: the hidden cost of delayed payment

**Working capital** is the money the group needs to keep producing while it waits to be paid. When a buyer pays 60 days after delivery, the group may have to fund two or three months of production from its own pocket. Many groups look only at the margin per piece and forget to ask whether they can survive the wait.
Worked example: testing a fashion retailer's offer

For example, Kemi's adire cooperative in Abeokuta, now registered, is offered a contract by a retailer: 300 pieces a month at 9,000 naira each, payment 60 days after each delivery, and the group may not sell to any other shop. The group's cost is 6,500 naira per piece and its working capital is 1,500,000 naira. Prices are illustrative.
Monthly production cost: 300 x 6,500 = 1,950,000 naira, which is already more than the group's 1,500,000.
Month 1's delivery is paid at the end of month 3. By then the group has funded 3 months: 3 x 1,950,000 = 5,850,000 naira.
The exclusivity clause would also stop sales to the group's existing customers, which threatens its independence.
Counter-offer drafted by the committee: 150 pieces a month, 30 percent deposit with each order, balance 30 days after delivery, no exclusivity, either side may end with 30 days' notice.
New order value: 150 x 9,000 = 1,350,000 naira. Deposit: 30 percent = 405,000. Cost: 150 x 6,500 = 975,000.
Net cash out per month: 975,000 - 405,000 = 570,000. Two months before the first balance arrives: 2 x 570,000 = 1,140,000 naira, within the 1,500,000 available.
Margin: 150 x (9,000 - 6,500) = 375,000 naira a month.

The original offer needed 5,850,000 naira of funding and took away the group's freedom to sell elsewhere. The counter-offer needs at most 1,140,000, keeps existing customers and still earns 375,000 naira a month. The committee takes both versions to a general meeting for a vote.

An attractive offer that takes control away from members should be renegotiated, not signed as it stands.
Terms to read twice
**Exclusivity:** stops you selling to others. Accept only with higher volumes, guaranteed for a fixed period.
**Penalties for late delivery:** check the amount and that it also applies to the buyer's late payment.
**Rejection of goods:** the buyer's quality standard should be written and match your specification sheet.
**Governance conditions from funders:** a funder may ask for reports and audits, which is reasonable, but should not appoint your officers or change your bylaws.
**Who signs:** only officers authorised by a committee or general meeting resolution, as your bylaws require.
Growing through cooperation among cooperatives

If an order is too big, Principle 6 offers another route: partner with another cooperative instead of overstretching your own. Two groups can split an order under a written agreement covering quality standard, share of the quantity, how payment flows, and who answers to the buyer. Cooperatives can also join together in a secondary body, often called a union, to buy inputs in bulk or market together. Ask your state cooperative office which unions operate in your sector.
Offers that are too good

Be cautious of "buyers" or "grant agents" who ask the group to pay a registration, processing or approval fee before an order or grant is released. Verify the organisation independently, never pay fees to a personal account, and take any such request to the committee before acting.

A cooperative is a group of peers, not a boss and workers. Leadership here rests on fair process and earned respect. Most serious crises in group enterprises can be traced to a weak point in the member lifecycle: a new member who never understood the rules, a quarrel left to grow for months, or a member who leaves and feels cheated. This lesson walks through each stage and gives you a calculation for a fair exit.
A person welcoming a new team member
A clear welcome and induction prevent many later disputes.
Admission and induction
The applicant reads the bylaws and the current group agreement, or has them read to her in her preferred language.
She completes an application form, which the secretary records in the membership register.
The committee or general meeting decides by the rule in the bylaws, applying the same criteria to every applicant, as Principle 1 requires.
She pays the entry fee and share capital into the group account and receives a receipt.
An experienced member takes her through the SOP, the specification sheet and the money rules in her first month.
At the end of the first month the production lead and the new member review her work together.
Education as a duty, not a favour

Principle 5 says cooperatives provide education and training for members, elected representatives, managers and employees, so they can contribute effectively to the cooperative's development. In practice, budget for it from the education fund set aside from surplus. Typical needs are bookkeeping for the treasurer and financial secretary, quality training for new producers, and short sessions for all members on reading the monthly statement. A member who can read the accounts is far less likely to suspect the officers without reason. Principle 5 also asks cooperatives to inform the public, particularly young people and opinion leaders, about the nature and benefits of cooperation. A short talk at a church, mosque or community meeting, explaining how your group works, is one practical way to do this, and it often brings in good new members.
The dispute and discipline ladder

Write a ladder into the bylaws and climb it one step at a time. Most issues end on the first or second step. Skipping straight to expulsion, or to a public argument in the WhatsApp group, usually makes things worse and can be challenged as unfair.
The dispute ladder

Mediation by a neutral member
Committee hearing, both sides heard
Written warning or sanction
General meeting decides expulsion
Each step is recorded; the member always has the right to be heard before a sanction.
The right to be heard

Before any sanction, tell the member in writing what she is accused of, give her a reasonable time to respond, and let her speak at the hearing. Record the decision and the reasons in the minutes. A process that skips this can split the group even when the accusation is true.
Exit: what a leaving member is owed

Members leave for many reasons: moving to another city, family needs, or disagreement. The bylaws should say what she receives and when. Usually she gets back her paid-up share capital, plus any patronage refund already declared but not yet paid, minus any money she owes the cooperative. Principle 3 notes that reserves are developed by the cooperative and that at least part of them should be indivisible. That means a leaving member does not take a share of the reserve fund. It stays to protect the members who remain.
Worked example: Ronke leaves the sewing cooperative
For example, Ronke is moving from Ibadan to Abuja and resigns from Bisola's cooperative. The bylaws say a leaving member is paid within 90 days of the committee accepting her resignation.
Paid-up share capital, confirmed in the members' ledger: 25,000 naira.
Patronage refund declared at the last general meeting and not yet paid: 18,400 naira.
Money she owes: the balance of an advance for a machine part, 12,000 naira.
Reserve fund: no share, because the bylaws make the reserve indivisible.
The financial secretary prepares a statement; Ronke and two officers sign it; the treasurer pays 31,400 naira by transfer to Ronke's own account and records the reference.

Ronke receives 31,400 naira with a signed statement showing exactly how it was calculated. Her name is removed from the membership register and the group's bank mandate if she was a signatory, and she leaves on good terms.
Plan exits so the group survives them

If several members could leave at once, paying out all their share capital might empty the account. Some bylaws allow payment in instalments or within a set period. Decide this calmly in the bylaws, not in the middle of a crisis.

Finally, mark successes together. When a big order is delivered or the audit comes back clean, say so at the meeting and record it in the minutes. Members who see shared success stay committed through the hard months.

The annual general meeting (AGM) is where the members, the highest authority in the cooperative, receive the accounts, approve the surplus allocation, elect officers and set direction. A well-run AGM is the clearest evidence that a group is a real cooperative and not a private business with members as helpers. This final lesson brings the course together: the report, the decisions and the plan that comes out of the meeting.

Notice and agenda

Send written notice to every member within the period your bylaws require, with the agenda and a short summary of the accounts, so members can read before the meeting. Share it on WhatsApp and also on paper for members who rely on it. Check quorum at the start and record it.

Running a fair election

Elections are where Principle 2 becomes visible. Announce which offices are vacant in the notice, so members can prepare. At the meeting, invite nominations, and let each candidate speak briefly. Choose two members who are not candidates to count the votes. Use a secret ballot on slips of paper when the post is contested, so nobody feels pressure to vote with a powerful relative or neighbour. Each member present has one vote, whatever her shares or how long she has been a member. The secretary records the names of candidates, votes for each and the winner in the minutes. Outgoing officers then hand over records, cash and bank access with a counted, signed handover note within an agreed period, for example two weeks, and the bank mandate is updated at once.

Principle 7 asks cooperatives to work for the sustainable development of their communities through policies approved by their members. The key words are "approved by their members". In the example, the 112,500 naira community fund is not spent by the chairperson's choice; the AGM votes on a proposal, such as paying the training costs of two young women from the community as apprentices with the group. Record the decision and report next year on what it achieved.

Is your group really a cooperative? Principles, form and bylaws
Is your group really a cooperative? Principles, legal form and bylaws.
This is the video for module one of Cooperative and Group Enterprise Management.
Why this matters
A cooperative is people, not capital
Autonomous: the group runs itself
Persons, not money, own the decisions
Voluntary: nobody is forced to join or stay
Jointly owned, democratically controlled
Many groups call themselves a cooperative. Some truly are. Others are one strong person's business with friends helping.
The International Cooperative Alliance, the global body for cooperatives, sets the standard. A cooperative is autonomous. A donor or buyer may support it, but does not control it.
It is an association of persons. The member with the biggest share does not own more of the decisions.
Members join voluntarily, to meet real shared needs.
And it is a real business, owned together and governed by the members.
How values become practice
Open membership, democratic control
Fair capital, surplus shared by use
Education and training
The seven principles put the values into practice. Membership is open, with written admission rules. And in primary cooperatives, it is one member, one vote, however many shares she holds.
Members contribute capital fairly. Surplus, the money left after costs, goes to reserves, to members according to their business with the cooperative, or to activities members approve.
Agreements with governments, buyers or funders must keep member control. For example, refuse a grant that would let the donor appoint your treasurer.
The last three: train members and leaders, work with other cooperatives, and serve your community.
Worked example
Bisola scores her sewing group
Open membership: 0
Democratic control: 0
Economic participation: 1
Education: 1
Other three principles: 2 each
Total: 8 out of 14. Fix membership and elections first.
For example, Bisola leads a 14-member sewing group in Ibadan. She scores each principle 2 if fully true, 1 if partly, 0 if not, out of 14.
New members join only if the founder likes them: 0. Officers were never elected, and the founder decides alone: 0.
Everyone paid the same 20,000 naira entry share, but surplus was never shared: 1. Two members learnt the machines, but nobody learnt bookkeeping: 1.
Autonomy, buying fabric with another group, and free uniform repairs for orphans score 2 each.
Total: 8 out of 14. Her weakest points are membership rules and democratic control, so her bylaws must fix admission and elections first.
Legal form
Who carries the risk?
Informal group
Not a legal person
Officers carry debts personally
Cheapest and fastest
A legal entity owned by members
Contracts in its own name
Registered at the state office

An informal group is fine while money is small. But it is not a legal person. If the treasurer signs for a 2 million naira fabric order and the buyer cancels, the supplier can chase the treasurer personally.
A cooperative society is registered with your state's cooperative office, not the Corporate Affairs Commission, and signs contracts in its own name.
Get current requirements and fees in writing from that office, and never pay an agent without an official receipt.
Readiness check
Written agreement, elected officers
Group bank account, two signatures
Weekly cashbook, recorded contributions
Monthly meetings with minutes
Disagreements and costs handled clearly
12 or more: go. 8 to 11: fix gaps for 90 days. Below 8: build.

Registration only gives trust a legal shape. So first score eight points: 2 if in place, 1 if partly, 0 if missing. Start with a written agreement, officers elected for a fixed term, and a group account needing two signatures.
Then a weekly cashbook, receipts for contributions, monthly meetings with minutes, an agreed way to settle disagreements, and a product with known costs.
Kemi's adire group in Abeokuta scored 10, because the money sat in the chairperson's personal account. So they spend about 90 days fixing gaps before registering.
Bylaws
Quorum and a two-thirds vote
24 members: quorum is half plus one, 13
18 members present: quorum met
Special resolution: two-thirds of 18 is 12
Vote: 13 yes, 4 no, 1 abstention
Record it all in the minutes
No quorum, no valid decision.
Bylaws are the rule book. A quorum is the minimum number of members who must be present for decisions to count. Serious matters need a special resolution, often two-thirds.
For example, Ngozi is secretary of a 24-member palm oil cooperative near Owerri.
Half of 24 is 12, plus one is 13. 18 members came, so quorum is met.
Buying a press on credit is a special resolution. Two-thirds of 18 is 12. The vote is 13 yes, so it passes.
Ngozi records members present, the motion and the vote count in the minutes.
Money rules
Protect members' money
All money in the group bank account
Two unrelated signatories per payment
Spending limits at three levels
Every naira in the cashbook
Never share PINs or one-time passwords

These money rules prevent most quarrels. No officer keeps group money in a personal account. Two signatories, not from the same household, approve each payment. Set spending limits, and record every naira with a receipt.
Never share the banking PIN or one-time passwords in the WhatsApp group. Confirm unusual requests by calling a saved number.
Key points
Remember
One member, one vote, whatever her shares
Score your group on all seven principles
Informal officers carry debts personally
Register at the state cooperative office
To remember. One member, one vote. Score your group honestly against all seven principles. In an informal group, officers carry the risk personally.
When you are ready, register with your state's cooperative office, with bylaws that set quorum, voting and money rules.

Roles, checks and fair sharing of the group's money
Roles, checks, and fair sharing of the group's money.
This is the video for module two of Cooperative and Group Enterprise Management.
Why this matters
Everybody's job is nobody's job
Give every task one named owner
Split every money process between two
Check quality and the bank every month
Share surplus by a written rule

In many groups, important tasks belong to everybody, which means nobody. Or one energetic member takes the order, collects the deposit, buys materials and keeps the records alone. Even if she is honest, the group cannot see what happened, and suspicion grows.
Separation of duties fixes this. Every money process is split between at least two people, so an error by one is likely to be noticed by another.
It is not an accusation. It protects an honest treasurer, because the records show what happened.
In this module you also check quality and the bank account every month, and share surplus fairly.
Order to cash
Hauwa's catering order, step by step
Sales lead sends a written quote
Deposit into the group account only
Treasurer confirms the payment
Bookkeeper records it with the reference
Production delivers, balance paid, receipt
Customer money never goes into a personal account.

A standard operating procedure, or SOP, is a one-page list of steps with an owner for each. For example, Hauwa's catering cooperative in Kaduna gets an order for 200 plates at 3,500 naira a plate. Aisha, the sales lead, sends a written quote for 700,000 naira.
The customer pays a 60 percent deposit of 420,000 naira into the cooperative's bank account. Aisha never accepts it into her own account.
Rakiya, the treasurer, confirms the credit on the bank app.
Zainab, the financial secretary, records it in the cashbook with the bank reference.
Hauwa leads production, and the balance of 280,000 naira is paid before the food is served. Five members, five clear duties, and every naira traceable.
Food safety
Food orders: hygiene in the SOP
Wash hands with soap and clean water
Separate raw and cooked foods
Cook thoroughly
Keep food at safe temperatures
Sick members do not handle food

If your group cooks or processes food, add hygiene to the SOP. These follow the WHO Five Keys to Safer Food. Wash hands with soap and clean water. Separate raw and cooked foods. Cook thoroughly, and keep food at safe temperatures.
A member with diarrhoea or vomiting should not handle food that day.
Quality
When work falls short
Do not
Post faults in the group chat
Quietly accept weak pieces
Do
Return pieces privately
Name the fault, set a date
Pair her with a stronger member

A buyer expects the same quality whoever made the item. So write a specification sheet clear enough that two members checking one item reach the same verdict. Then inspect each batch and record the results.
Never criticise weak work publicly on WhatsApp.
Return faulty pieces privately, with the fault named, for example hem uneven by 2 cm, and a date to correct it. If she fails twice, pair her with a stronger member.
Bank reconciliation
Make the cashbook match the bank
Bank charges not yet recorded
Payments that reached the bank unrecorded
Deposits the bank shows the next day
Mistakes, such as a line written twice
Every month, compare the cashbook balance with the bank statement for the same date, and explain every difference.
For example, Grace in Jos found the cashbook at 412,500 naira and the bank at 389,000. First, bank charges and SMS fees of 1,500 naira were missing.
A member's 20,000 naira share payment was never written down, and a 45,000 naira deposit showed at the bank a day later.
The last 3,000 naira was a thread payment written twice. Both sides then showed 434,000 naira, and two people signed.
If money is still missing, do not accuse anyone in the group chat. The supervisory committee asks privately and reports to the general meeting.
Worked example
Costing 300 uniform sets
For example, Bisola's 6 sewing members are offered 300 uniform sets at 6,500 naira a set.
Order value
Materials
Sewing labour paid to members
Total cost, all lines
Surplus. Naira prices are illustrative.
Now cost an order. Members' labour is a real cost. If the price only covers materials, members are working for nothing.
The order is worth 1,950,000 naira. Materials cost 855,000, and sewing labour paid to members is 450,000. With cutting, transport, fuel and bank fees, total costs come to 1,470,000 naira.
That leaves a surplus of 480,000 naira.
Capacity check: 30 sets a day means 10 days, plus a 20 percent buffer is 12 days. That fits the 15-day deadline, so they accept.
Sharing the surplus
Split it by the bylaws
120,000 naira builds the cooperative's reserve.
24,000 naira pays for members' training.
336,000 naira, or 1,120 naira for each set a member sewed.
Share the surplus by the rule in your bylaws. In this example, 25 percent, 120,000 naira, goes to the reserve.
5 percent, 24,000 naira, goes to training.
And 70 percent is a patronage refund, shared by how much each member did: 1,120 naira per set. Bisola sewed 70 sets and gets 78,400 naira. Shade sewed 30 and gets 33,600.
Share only after the customer has paid in full, and never change the rule after the figures are known.
Key points
Remember
One named owner for every task
Two people in every money process
Reconcile with the bank every month
Labour is a cost; share surplus by the rule

To remember. Give every task one owner. Split every money process between two people. Reconcile with the bank monthly. And count members' labour as a cost before you share any surplus by the written rule.

Grow without losing control: offers, members and the AGM
Grow without losing control: big offers, members, and the AGM.
This is the video for module three of Cooperative and Group Enterprise Management.
Why this matters
Good attention, risky terms
Big buyers want your group's capacity
Some terms can sink a small cooperative
Members must keep control
Fair process keeps members together
A well-run group attracts bigger buyers, distributors and programmes, because it offers more capacity than one producer.
But large offers can come with long payment delays, exclusivity, penalties, or a partner who wants a say in how the group is run.
Principle 4 says any outside agreement must keep democratic control by the members. And inside, a fair member lifecycle and an honest AGM keep the group together.
Four questions
Test every big offer
Cash: what must we spend before payment?
Capacity: can we deliver, with a 20 percent buffer?
Control: does any clause give away power?
Exit: can either side end it with notice?
Never pay a fee to release an order or grant.
Ask four questions before members vote. Cash: how much must the group spend before the first payment arrives? This is working capital, the money you need to keep producing while you wait to be paid.
Capacity: can we produce this quantity, to the standard, with a 20 percent time buffer?
Control: does any clause give the partner power over our members, officers, prices or bylaws?
Exit: can either side end it with reasonable notice?
And be cautious of buyers or grant agents who ask for a processing fee first. Verify them independently, and never pay fees to a personal account.
Worked example
Kemi's adire offer and counter-offer
Retailer's offer
300 pieces a month
Paid 60 days after delivery
No sales to other shops
Needs 5,850,000 naira
Counter-offer
150 pieces a month
30 percent deposit with each order
No exclusivity, 30 days' notice
Needs at most 1,140,000 naira

For example, a retailer offers Kemi's adire cooperative 300 pieces a month at 9,000 naira each, paid 60 days after delivery, with no sales to any other shop. Each piece costs 6,500 naira, and the group has 1,500,000 naira of working capital.
Monthly cost is 1,950,000 naira. By the first payment, the group would have funded 5,850,000 naira.
So the committee drafts a counter-offer: 150 pieces a month, a 30 percent deposit, the balance 30 days after delivery, and no exclusivity.
That needs at most 1,140,000 naira, keeps existing customers, and still earns 375,000 naira a month. Both versions go to a general meeting vote.
Member lifecycle
From admission to exit
Same written admission rules for all
Induction by an experienced member
Training paid from the education fund
Disputes climb a ladder, step by step
Most crises trace back to a weak point in the member lifecycle. Apply the same written admission criteria to every applicant, and read her the bylaws in her preferred language.
In her first month, an experienced member takes her through the SOP, the specification sheet and the money rules.
Training is a duty under Principle 5. A member who can read the accounts is far less likely to suspect the officers without reason.
For disputes, start with a private conversation, then mediation, then a committee hearing. Before any sanction, the member always has the right to be heard.
What a leaving member is owed
For example, Ronke is moving from Ibadan to Abuja and resigns from Bisola's cooperative.
Paid-up share capital
Declared refund not yet paid
Minus: advance she owes
No share of the reserve. Figures illustrative.
When a member leaves, she usually gets back her share capital, plus any declared refund not yet paid, minus what she owes.
Ronke paid 25,000 naira in share capital, is owed an 18,400 naira refund, and still owes 12,000 naira for a machine part.
So she receives 31,400 naira, with a signed statement, by transfer to her own account.
She does not take a share of the reserve. The bylaws make it indivisible, so it stays to protect the members who remain.
The AGM
Three jobs at the annual meeting
Sales, costs, surplus and an allocation that adds back exactly. Kemi's group: 750 naira per piece.
Two non-candidates count. Secret ballot when contested. One member, one vote.
The community fund is spent on a proposal members approve, not by the chairperson's choice.

At the annual general meeting, members receive the accounts, approve the surplus allocation and elect officers. Kemi's group had a surplus of 2,250,000 naira. The patronage refund came to 750 naira per piece, so each member can check her own refund.
For elections, choose two members who are not candidates to count, and use a secret ballot when a post is contested.
Under Principle 7, the community fund is spent only on a proposal the members vote for, such as training two young women as apprentices.
After the AGM
Every action needs an owner, a date and evidence.
End the AGM by agreeing your single biggest governance gap, such as no two-signatory account or no written surplus rule.
Draft the fix, consult members, and vote on it at a meeting.
Then apply it, check it, and report back on day 90.
Key points
Remember
Test offers on cash, capacity, control, exit
Counter-offer with deposits, no exclusivity
Let every member be heard before sanctions
Reserves stay; members decide at the AGM
To remember. Test every offer on cash, capacity, control and exit, and counter-offer when needed. Treat members fairly from admission to exit. And let the AGM, the members, decide.
